understanding.title: Understanding UUIDs
understanding.p1: A UUID — Universally Unique Identifier — is a 128-bit value written as 32 hexadecimal characters split into five groups of 8-4-4-4-12. With its four hyphens it is exactly 36 characters long, which is why you see it everywhere from database columns to log lines.
understanding.p2: The reason UUIDs exist is coordination-free uniqueness. Any process, on any machine, can mint one without asking a central authority for the next number in a sequence. Two services that have never spoken to each other can generate identifiers all day and still never collide in practice.
understanding.p3: The layout is standardised by RFC 9562, which superseded the long-serving RFC 4122. Two fields are fixed by the spec: the version nibble, which is the first character of the third group, and the variant bits at the start of the fourth group. Everything else is filled by the version's own algorithm.

why.title: Why use UUIDs
why.p1: Auto-incrementing integers are compact and readable, but they force every writer through a single source of truth. UUIDs remove that bottleneck: a mobile client can create records while offline, a queue consumer can assign ids before the row exists, and two shards can merge without renumbering anything.
why.p2: They are also safer to expose. A sequential id in a URL quietly publishes how many records you have and lets anyone walk your dataset by counting upwards. A UUID reveals neither.
why.p3: The trade-offs are real and worth naming. A UUID takes 16 bytes against 8 for a bigint, and 36 bytes if you store the text form. Fully random v4 values also scatter B-tree inserts across the whole index, which hurts write throughput on large tables. Version 7 was standardised precisely to solve that second problem.

types.title: Types of UUIDs
types.intro: RFC 9562 defines eight versions. Three of them cover almost every real use case, and those are the three this generator produces.
types.tableCaption: Comparison of the UUID versions offered by ToolForge
types.v1BestFor: Legacy systems that already expect v1
types.v4BestFor: General purpose ids, tokens, correlation keys
types.v7BestFor: Database primary keys and event streams
types.others: The remaining versions are niche: v3 and v5 hash a name into a namespace deterministically, v6 reorders the v1 timestamp so it sorts correctly, and v8 is a deliberately open slot for vendor-specific layouts.

howItWorks.title: How our generator works
howItWorks.p1: Every identifier on this page is produced by the Web Crypto API — specifically crypto.getRandomValues, the same cryptographically secure source your browser uses for TLS. There is no server call, no queue, and no fallback to Math.random.
howItWorks.p2: Version 7 gets one extra guarantee. When several ids are minted inside the same millisecond, the twelve rand_a bits are used as a dedicated counter rather than random noise, following the monotonicity method in RFC 9562. A batch of 500 therefore comes back in strictly ascending order.
howItWorks.p3: Because the work happens locally, the values you see were never transmitted, never logged, and never stored. Load the page once and it keeps working with the network switched off. The batch size is capped at 500 so a single generation stays imperceptible even on a low-powered device.

useCases.title: Use cases
useCases.p1: The most common use is a primary key. Version 7 is the better choice here: it keeps inserts clustered at the right edge of the index the way a sequence would, while still being generated by the client.
useCases.p2: Idempotency keys are the second big one. Attach a fresh UUID to a payment or a webhook retry and the receiving service can safely discard duplicates without any shared state.
useCases.p3: Beyond persistence, UUIDs are the default for correlation and trace ids that stitch a request together across services, for object-storage keys that must not collide between uploaders, and for seeded test fixtures where a readable, guaranteed-unique value beats a hand-written string.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Can two UUIDs ever be the same?
faq.a1: Mathematically yes, practically no. A version 4 UUID has 122 random bits. You would need to generate roughly 2.7 × 10^18 of them before reaching a one-in-a-billion chance of a single collision.
faq.a2: Version 7 for anything stored in an indexed column, version 4 for everything else. Only reach for version 1 when an existing system already depends on its layout.
faq.q3: Are these UUIDs safe to use as security tokens?
faq.a3: Version 4 UUIDs from this page are backed by a cryptographically secure random source, so they are unguessable. Versions 1 and 7 embed a readable timestamp, so treat them as identifiers rather than secrets.
faq.q4: Is anything I generate sent to your servers?
faq.a4: No. The generator is client-side JavaScript. The page makes no network request while generating, and nothing you copy or download is ever transmitted.

understanding.title: Understanding Base64
understanding.p1: Base64 is a binary-to-text encoding. It takes arbitrary bytes and rewrites them using 64 printable ASCII characters — A–Z, a–z, 0–9 and two symbols — so the data can travel through any channel that only understands text.
understanding.p2: The scheme works in groups of three bytes. Twenty-four bits divide evenly into four six-bit numbers, and each number selects one character from the alphabet. When the input does not divide by three, the final group is padded with one or two = characters so the output length stays a multiple of four.
understanding.p3: That regularity is the whole point. Base64 is neither compression nor encryption: anyone can decode it, and the result is always about a third larger than what went in. It exists so bytes survive a trip through systems that would otherwise mangle them.

why.title: Why encode to Base64
why.p1: Plenty of formats are text-only by design. Email bodies, JSON payloads, XML documents, HTTP headers and YAML files all expect characters rather than raw bytes. Drop a PNG straight into any of them and the first byte outside the printable range breaks the parser.
why.p2: Base64 gives those bytes a safe disguise. An image can be embedded in a stylesheet, a certificate can be pasted into a config file, and a binary attachment can move through a mail server written decades ago — none of which needed changing.
why.p3: The cost is size and readability. A megabyte of input becomes roughly 1.37 MB of output, and no human can read it. Reach for it when the channel demands text, not out of habit: if you control both ends and they speak binary, send binary.

variants.title: Variants of Base64
variants.intro: The variants in daily use differ in only two places — the last two characters of the alphabet, and whether the output carries its padding.
variants.tableCaption: Comparison of the Base64 variants ToolForge produces
variants.standardBestFor: MIME, email, and most APIs and libraries
variants.dataUriBestFor: Inline images in CSS, HTML, and Markdown
variants.others: RFC 4648 also defines base32 and base16 for cases where case-insensitivity matters more than density. Despite the different name, base64url is the same encoding — only the two final symbols change, so a decoder that accepts both, like this one, never has to be told which it is reading.

options.title: Every option, and when to use it
options.intro: The defaults — UTF-8, standard alphabet, padded, one continuous payload — are what you want most of the time. The rest of the controls exist for the cases where the receiving system is stricter, older, or expects a particular shape.
options.tableCaption: What each converter option does and when it is worth turning on
options.charsetDoes: Decides how text becomes bytes when encoding, and how bytes become text when decoding.
options.charsetWhen: The data is not UTF-8 — a Windows-1252 spreadsheet export, an ISO-8859-2 dump, a Shift_JIS log.
options.newlineDoes: Rewrites every line break in the result to LF, CRLF, or CR, whatever the input used.
options.newlineWhen: The receiver is strict about it, such as Windows tooling or a protocol that demands CRLF.
options.perLineDoes: Converts one line at a time instead of treating the whole box as a single payload.
options.perLineWhen: You have a list — one token, id, or string per line — and want a result for each.
options.urlSafeDoes: Swaps the final two alphabet characters, + and /, for - and _.
options.urlSafeWhen: The result goes into a URL, a filename, or a JWT segment.
options.paddingDoes: Adds the trailing = characters so the length is always a multiple of four.
options.paddingWhen: The receiver expects it. Leave it off for base64url, which conventionally drops it.
options.wrapDoes: Folds the encoded output into 76-character lines.
options.wrapWhen: You are writing a MIME body or a PEM-style block, both of which expect wrapped text.
options.dataUriDoes: Prefixes the payload with data:'<type>';base64, using the file's own media type.
options.dataUriWhen: The result is going straight into CSS, HTML, or Markdown as an inline asset.
options.charsetNote: Two things about character sets are worth knowing. Encoding can only write a set this page can also invert, so the multi-byte East Asian sets — Shift_JIS, GBK, GB18030, Big5, EUC-JP, EUC-KR — are offered when decoding but not when encoding. And a set narrower than your text will say so: type an emoji with ASCII selected and you get the exact position that cannot be written, rather than a silently corrupted byte.
options.defaultsNote: The options also constrain each other, and the interface follows suit rather than producing something broken. A data URI describes one continuous standard-alphabet payload, so switching on URL-safe, line wrapping, or per-line conversion greys it out. Encoding a file ignores the character set and line endings entirely, because a file is already bytes and has no line structure to normalise.

howItWorks.title: How our converter works
howItWorks.p1: Everything on this page runs on your device. The encoder walks the input three bytes at a time and emits four characters per group; the decoder does the reverse, folding four characters back into three bytes. There is no server call and nothing is stored.
howItWorks.p2: Text becomes bytes before it is encoded, and which bytes depends on the source character set. UTF-8 is the default and the only one that carries every script; pick Windows-1252 or ISO-8859-2 and anything outside that set is reported rather than silently mangled. Decoding applies the same choice in reverse, so a payload written in Shift_JIS reads back as Japanese instead of mojibake. Converters built on the browser's own btoa can do none of this — btoa throws on any character above U+00FF.
howItWorks.p3: The decoder is deliberately forgiving. It reads either alphabet, ignores line breaks and spaces, tolerates missing padding, and strips a data: URI header when it finds one. What it will not do is guess: a character outside the alphabet is reported with its exact position instead of being silently dropped. Lists can be converted a line at a time, line endings rewritten to LF, CRLF or CR, and encoded output folded at 76 characters the way a MIME body expects.

useCases.title: Use cases
useCases.p1: Data URIs are the most visible use. A small icon encoded into a stylesheet saves a request, and an inline preview needs no upload at all.
useCases.p2: Credentials and keys are the second. HTTP Basic auth is a Base64 pair, JWT headers and payloads are base64url, and PEM certificates are Base64 wrapped at 64 columns between BEGIN and END lines.
useCases.p3: Beyond that: attaching files to a JSON API with no multipart endpoint, storing small blobs in a column that only accepts text, and moving binaries through logs, webhooks, or a paste into a terminal.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is Base64 a form of encryption?
faq.a1: No. It is a reversible encoding with no key, and every language ships a decoder. Anything you encode is readable by anyone who receives it, so never use it to hide a secret.
faq.q2: Why is the encoded output bigger than my file?
faq.a2: Every three bytes become four characters, so the output grows by about a third, plus up to two padding characters. That overhead is inherent to the encoding and cannot be tuned away.
faq.q3: What is the difference between Base64 and base64url?
faq.a3: Only the last two characters of the alphabet. Standard Base64 uses + and /, both of which mean something inside a URL; base64url swaps them for - and _ and usually drops the = padding. Turn on URL-safe above to produce it.
faq.a4: No. Files are read with the browser's File API and converted on your device. The page makes no network request while converting, and nothing you paste, open, or download is ever transmitted.
faq.q5: Which character set should I pick?
faq.a5: UTF-8 unless you know otherwise — it covers every script and is what the modern web assumes. Reach for another only when the data itself predates that: a Windows-1252 spreadsheet export, an ISO-8859-2 dump, a Shift_JIS log. If a decode comes back as mojibake, the destination character set is usually the thing to change.
faq.q6: Why does my output have line breaks in it?
faq.a6: Either “Split at 76 chars” is on, which folds the payload the way a MIME body needs, or “Each line separately” is on, which emits one result per input line. Both are off by default; turning them off gives you a single continuous string again.

understanding.title: What a JSON Web Token actually is
understanding.p1: A JSON Web Token is a compact, URL-safe way to carry a set of claims — statements such as who a user is, what they may do, and when the statement stops being true. RFC 7519 defines the format; RFC 7515 defines the signature that makes it trustworthy.
understanding.p2: The value you paste into this tool is a JWS: three base64url-encoded parts joined by dots. The first two are JSON objects, plainly readable by anyone. The third is a signature over the first two, which is what turns a readable blob into something a server can rely on.
understanding.p3: That split explains most of what people find surprising about JWTs. Reading one requires nothing. Trusting one requires the key. The tool above keeps those two jobs visibly separate, because conflating them is where real systems go wrong.

anatomy.title: The three parts
anatomy.intro: Each part is base64url with its padding stripped, so a token survives being pasted into a URL, a header, or a cookie without further escaping.
anatomy.tableCaption: The three segments of a JWS and what each contributes
anatomy.headerHolds: How the token was signed: alg, typ, and often a kid naming the key.
anatomy.headerSigned: Yes — altering it invalidates the signature.
anatomy.payloadHolds: The claims themselves: registered ones such as sub and exp, plus anything the issuer adds.
anatomy.payloadSigned: Yes — altering it invalidates the signature.
anatomy.signatureHolds: The MAC or signature over the first two parts, joined by a dot.
anatomy.encoding: Base64url is an encoding, not a cipher. Decoding a payload takes no key and no permission — which is why the same claim data must never include anything you would not print in a log.

claims.title: The registered claims
claims.intro: RFC 7519 reserves seven claim names. None is mandatory, but a token that omits exp has no way to stop being valid, and one that omits iss and aud is hard to scope to a single service.
claims.tableCaption: Registered JWT claims and what each carries
claims.issDetail: Identifies who minted the token, so a verifier can pick the right key and reject tokens from anyone else.
claims.subDetail: Identifies the principal the claims are about — usually a user id, and unique within the issuer.
claims.audDetail: Names the recipients the token is for. A service that finds itself absent from aud must reject the token.
claims.expDetail: Seconds since the Unix epoch after which the token must be rejected. The single most important claim to include.
claims.nbfDetail: Seconds since the epoch before which the token must be rejected — useful for credentials issued ahead of time.
claims.iatDetail: When the token was created. Lets a verifier reject anything older than it is willing to accept, independently of exp.
claims.jtiDetail: A unique identifier for the token, so a replayed copy can be spotted and refused.
claims.privateClaims: Everything else is a public or private claim, named by whoever issues the token. Prefixing your own claims with a URI or a short vendor namespace keeps them from colliding with a future registered name.

algorithms.title: Signing algorithms
algorithms.intro: The alg header names one entry from the JOSE registry. The families differ in what the verifier needs to hold: a copy of the signing secret, or only a public key.
algorithms.tableCaption: JWS algorithm families supported by this tool
algorithms.hmacKey: One shared secret, used to sign and to verify.
algorithms.hmacWhen: The same service issues and checks the token, so there is no third party to keep a secret from.
algorithms.rsaKey: Private key to sign, public key to verify.
algorithms.rsaWhen: Verifiers are separate services, or outside your control, and you need the widest possible library support.
algorithms.rsaPssKey: Private key to sign, public key to verify.
algorithms.rsaPssWhen: You want the modern RSA padding and control both ends well enough to know PS is supported.
algorithms.ecdsaKey: Private key to sign, public key to verify.
algorithms.ecdsaWhen: You want asymmetric verification with far smaller keys and signatures than RSA.
algorithms.eddsaKey: Private key to sign, public key to verify.
algorithms.eddsaWhen: You control the stack and want the fastest, simplest modern signature — Ed25519 under the hood.
algorithms.noneNote: The registry also lists none, an unsigned token. This tool decodes those and flags them loudly, but will not issue one: a token with no signature is a claim with no evidence, and verifiers that trusted the header's algorithm are exactly how that became a documented attack.
algorithms.sizeNote: For HMAC, RFC 7518 asks for a key at least as long as the hash: 32 bytes for HS256, 48 for HS384, 64 for HS512. A shorter secret still produces a valid-looking token, which is why the workbench points it out rather than quietly accepting it.

verifying.title: How verification actually works
verifying.p1: Verifying recomputes the signature over the first two segments, exactly as they appear in the token, and compares it with the third. This is why the tool signs a compacted copy of your payload rather than the indented text in the editor: the bytes that were signed are the bytes that must be checked.
verifying.p2: The order matters. Check the structure, then the signature, then the claims. A token whose exp has passed is worth rejecting, but only after you know the exp you are reading is one the issuer actually wrote.
verifying.p3: The rule worth carrying away: never verify with the algorithm the token asks for. Pass your verifier an explicit list of algorithms you accept. A verifier that reads alg from the header can be handed an RS256 token rewritten as HS256, signed with the very public key it publishes — the public key becomes the HMAC secret, and the forgery verifies.
verifying.p4: That is why the decoder above shows an expected-algorithm control instead of silently following the header. It starts from what the token declares, then checks against your choice, and says so plainly when the two disagree.

options.title: Every control on this page
options.intro: The workbench has two directions and a small set of controls shared between them.
options.tableCaption: Controls in the JWT workbench, what each does, and when to use it
options.modeDoes: Switches between reading a token and signing one.
options.modeWhen: You have a token to inspect, or claims you want to turn into one.
options.exampleDoes: Signs a sample token, minting a throwaway key pair for the asymmetric families.
options.exampleWhen: You want to try RS, PS, ES or EdDSA without having a key pair to hand.
options.viewDoes: Swaps the decoded panels between raw JSON and a table that names each claim and dates the time claims.
options.viewWhen: You want the exact bytes, or you want to know what exp is actually saying.
options.expectedAlgorithmDoes: Fixes the one algorithm the signature is checked against, and swaps the key box to match.
options.expectedAlgorithmWhen: Always. Leave it on the token's own value to confirm a signature; change it to see a mismatch reported.
options.secretDoes: Holds the shared secret for the HMAC family.
options.secretWhen: The token's alg starts with HS.
options.base64urlDoes: Decodes the secret from base64 to raw bytes before use, instead of taking the text's own bytes.
options.base64urlWhen: Your issuer stores its secret as base64 — most generated secrets are. Getting this wrong is the usual cause of a signature that will not match.
options.pemDoes: Accepts a public key or certificate for verifying, and a PKCS#8 private key for signing.
options.pemWhen: The token's alg starts with RS, PS, ES, or is EdDSA.
options.downloadDoes: Saves the decoded header, payload and signature as JSON, or the signed token as a text file.
options.downloadWhen: You want the result in a fixture file rather than on the clipboard.
options.headerOwnsAlg: In the encoder, the header is the single source of truth for alg. The algorithm select writes into it rather than sitting beside it, so there is never a second value to fall out of step — edit the header directly and the signing algorithm follows.
options.noTokenParam: There is deliberately no way to put a token in this page's URL. A JWT is a bearer credential, and a URL ends up in browser history, proxy logs, server access logs, and the Referer header of every outbound link. Only the mode and the algorithm travel in a link.

pitfalls.title: What goes wrong in practice
pitfalls.p1: Encoded is not encrypted. Every claim in a JWT is readable by anyone who holds the token, including the user it was issued to. Email addresses, internal ids and role names all leak by design; passwords and API keys in a payload are a live incident, not a code-review nit.
pitfalls.p2: Signatures do not expire on their own. A token stays valid until its exp passes, and there is no way to call it back before then. Anything you might need to withdraw quickly — a session, an elevated role — needs either a short life or a revocation list the verifier actually checks.
pitfalls.p3: The algorithm is an attacker-controlled field until you pin it. Accept an explicit allowlist in your verifier and treat everything else, none included, as a rejected token.
pitfalls.p4: Header parameters that name a key are equally attacker-controlled. jku, jwk and x5u ask a verifier to fetch or trust key material chosen by the token; unless you are certain your library ignores them, assume a token carrying them is trying something.
pitfalls.p5: Where the token lives matters as much as what is in it. localStorage is readable by any script on the page, which turns one cross-site scripting bug into stolen credentials. Prefer a cookie with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite set, and keep the lifetime short.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.a1: No. Decoding, signing and verification all run in your browser through the Web Crypto API. There is no request to any server, which is also why the tool works with the network switched off. The page has no way to put a token in its URL either, so nothing lands in browser history or server logs.
faq.a2: No. A standard JWT is signed, which proves it was not altered — it does not hide anything. The header and payload are base64url, an encoding anyone can reverse in one line of code. If the contents must stay private, you want a JWE, the five-part encrypted format, which this tool identifies but cannot open.
faq.q3: Why does my signature not verify?
faq.a3: Usually the secret is right but its form is wrong. Many issuers store an HMAC secret as base64, and signing with the letters of that string is not the same as signing with the bytes it encodes — the Base64url encoded switch decides which one is used. Otherwise: check that the expected algorithm matches the header, that an RSA or EC key is the public half rather than the private one, and that the token was not truncated in a copy.
faq.q4: Can I create a token with alg: none?
faq.a4: The decoder reads them and flags them, but the encoder will not issue one. An unsigned token is a set of claims with no evidence behind them, and verifiers that trusted the header's algorithm turned that into a documented attack. If you need one to test a defence, produce it deliberately in your own test code rather than from a public page.
faq.q5: What key format does the tool accept?
faq.a5: HMAC takes a plain secret, optionally base64url encoded. The RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA families take PEM: a PUBLIC KEY or CERTIFICATE block for verifying, and a PKCS#8 PRIVATE KEY block for signing. PKCS#1 blocks, the ones beginning BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY, are not supported by Web Crypto — convert with openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt -in key.pem.
faq.q6: How long should a token live?
faq.a6: Short enough that a stolen copy stops working before it is useful, and long enough not to fight your refresh flow. Minutes for an access token is a common answer; days is a decision to make deliberately. The workbench flags a token with no exp at all, and notes one whose expiry is far enough out that revocation becomes your only way to withdraw it.

understanding.title: What a hash actually is
understanding.p1: A hash function takes any amount of input and returns a fixed-length value. The same input always gives the same output, and there is no way to run it backwards — the only way to find an input that produces a given hash is to try inputs until one does. That one-way property is what makes hashes useful for checking things rather than storing them.
understanding.p2: Two properties matter in practice. Preimage resistance means that, given a hash, you cannot work out an input that produces it. Collision resistance means you cannot find two different inputs that hash to the same value. MD5 and SHA-1 still have their preimage resistance intact, but their collision resistance is thoroughly broken — which is why they survive as checksums and have no business anywhere near a signature.
understanding.p3: Password hashing is a different job wearing the same word. A digest is designed to be fast, and an attacker with a stolen database wants exactly that speed. bcrypt and Argon2 are built to be slow and memory-hungry on purpose, and they salt every hash so two identical passwords do not produce the same stored value.

choosing.title: Choosing an algorithm
choosing.intro: The single most consequential choice here is whether you are hashing data or a password. Everything else follows from that.
choosing.tableCaption: Hash algorithms, what each is for, and what each should not be used for
choosing.md5UseFor: Checking a file against a published checksum, or keying a cache where nobody is trying to fool you.
choosing.md5Avoid: Signatures, certificates, deduplication, or anything an attacker can influence. Colliding MD5 inputs can be produced in seconds.
choosing.sha1UseFor: Reading legacy systems that already emit it — Git object ids, older TLS chains.
choosing.sha1Avoid: Anything new. Collisions have been demonstrated in practice since 2017.
choosing.sha256UseFor: The general-purpose default: content addressing, integrity checks, HMAC keys, signature digests.
choosing.sha256Avoid: Storing passwords. It is fast, and speed is the attacker's advantage.
choosing.sha512UseFor: The same work as SHA-256 where a longer digest is required, or on 64-bit hardware where it is often faster.
choosing.sha512Avoid: Storing passwords, for exactly the same reason.
choosing.bcryptUseFor: Storing passwords in a system that already uses it, or where you need a format every language has a library for.
choosing.bcryptAvoid: Passphrases longer than 72 bytes, which it silently truncates. Use Argon2id instead.
choosing.argon2UseFor: New systems storing passwords. Argon2id is the current first recommendation, and resists both GPU and side-channel attacks.
choosing.argon2Avoid: Hashing large files or high-volume data — it is slow and memory-hungry by design.
choosing.variantsNote: Argon2 comes in three variants. Argon2id is the one to pick: it runs the memory-hard, side-channel-resistant Argon2i for its first half pass and the faster, GPU-resistant Argon2d for the rest. Argon2i and Argon2d are here for reproducing hashes that already exist, not for new work.
choosing.shaNote: SHA-1 and SHA-256 are unrelated designs despite the shared name; SHA-256 and SHA-512 are the same design at different widths. None of them is a password hash.

passwords.title: Why a fast hash is the wrong tool for a password
passwords.p1: Suppose a database of SHA-256 password hashes leaks. A consumer graphics card computes billions of SHA-256 hashes a second, so an attacker works through every eight-character password in hours, and every word in every leaked-password list in minutes. The hash function did nothing wrong — it was fast, which is what it was built to be.
passwords.p2: bcrypt and Argon2 attack this from the other side. A cost factor sets how much work one hash takes, and you raise it as hardware gets faster. bcrypt's cost is exponential: each step doubles the rounds, so cost 12 is four times the work of cost 10. Argon2 adds a memory cost, which matters because memory is the one resource a GPU cannot cheaply multiply — a card with thousands of cores and a few gigabytes of RAM cannot run thousands of 64 MiB hashes at once.
passwords.p3: Both salt automatically. A salt is a random value mixed into the hash and stored alongside it, so two people with the same password get different stored hashes, and a precomputed table built for one database is useless against another. You never need to generate or manage a salt yourself — it lives inside the $-delimited string the algorithm hands back.
passwords.p4: That string is the whole record. `$2b$10$` followed by 53 characters carries the bcrypt version, the cost, the salt, and the hash. `$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$…` carries the variant, the Argon2 version, all three cost parameters, the salt, and the hash. Store that one string and any correct implementation can verify a password against it years later, whatever settings you have moved on to.
passwords.p5: Never paste a password you actually use into any web tool, including this one. This page runs entirely in your browser and sends nothing anywhere, but that is a property you would have to verify rather than trust. Use it with test passwords.

options.title: Every setting, and when it matters
options.intro: Which settings appear depends on the algorithm. A setting that cannot apply is disabled with a note saying why, rather than being quietly ignored.
options.tableCaption: Every setting in the workbench, what it does, and when to reach for it
options.modeDoes: Switches between producing a hash and checking one.
options.modeWhen: You already have a hash and want to know whether something matches it.
options.algorithmDoes: Picks the hash function, and with it which settings below apply.
options.algorithmWhen: Always. The digest and password families behave completely differently.
options.encodingDoes: Writes a raw digest as hex or as base64.
options.encodingWhen: You are matching a system that publishes base64 digests — Subresource Integrity attributes and many package lock files do.
options.uppercaseDoes: Capitalises hex output. Disabled under base64, which is case-significant.
options.uppercaseWhen: You are comparing against a checksum file that publishes capitals. The value is the same either way.
options.costDoes: Sets bcrypt's work factor. The round count is two to this power.
options.costWhen: Matching an existing system's setting, or working out what your servers can carry. 10 to 12 is the usual range.
options.memoryDoes: Sets how much memory one Argon2 hash must hold, in KiB.
options.memoryWhen: This is Argon2's main defence. Raise it as far as your servers allow before raising iterations.
options.iterationsDoes: Sets how many passes Argon2 makes over that memory.
options.iterationsWhen: You have hit your memory ceiling and still want more work per hash.
options.parallelismDoes: Splits the memory into that many lanes.
options.parallelismWhen: Matching a hash that already specifies it. Memory must be at least 8 KiB per lane.
options.hashLengthDoes: Sets how many bytes of Argon2 output to keep.
options.hashLengthWhen: Matching an existing format. 32 bytes is the common choice and there is little reason to change it.
options.newSaltDoes: Draws fresh random bytes for the salted families, so the same input hashes to something different.
options.newSaltWhen: You want to see that bcrypt and Argon2 never produce the same hash twice for the same password.
options.downloadDoes: Saves the current result as a timestamped text file.
options.downloadWhen: You are recording a checksum alongside a release artefact.
options.saltNote: The digests take no salt at all, so the salt control does nothing under MD5 or the SHA family and is disabled there. This is not a shortcoming of those algorithms — a checksum has to be reproducible by anyone with the same file, which is exactly what a salt prevents.
options.costNote: The cost factor is capped at 14 here rather than bcrypt's own 31. Hashing runs in this tab, on the same thread that draws the page, and each step doubles the time — cost 14 already takes about a second, and cost 31 would take longer than the machine will be switched on. Production systems are not bound by that cap; a server can run cost 12 comfortably.
options.defaultsNote: The defaults are SHA-256 in lower-case hex, bcrypt at cost 10, and Argon2id at 19456 KiB with two iterations on one lane — the current OWASP first-choice setting.

comparing.title: How comparing works
comparing.intro: There is one rule, and the right-hand box decides everything.
comparing.p1: Whatever you paste on the right is read first. If it is a bcrypt or Argon2 hash, every parameter needed to check it — cost, memory, iterations, lanes, salt — is already inside that string, so the tool reads them back out and uses them. Nothing in the Generate settings affects a comparison, which is what lets you verify a hash made with settings you no longer use.
comparing.p2: If the right-hand box holds a bare digest instead, its length identifies the algorithm: 32 hex characters is MD5, 40 is SHA-1, 64 is SHA-256, 128 is SHA-512, and base64 has its own four widths. Length is the only signal a bare digest carries. Thirty-two hex characters is equally an MD5, an MD4, or an NTLM hash, and no tool can tell them apart from the string alone.
comparing.p3: With a digest on the right, what is on the left decides which of two checks runs. If the left box holds a digest of exactly the same algorithm and encoding, the two are compared directly — the checksum-against-checksum case. Otherwise the left box is treated as text, hashed with the detected algorithm, and the results are compared. The tool always names which of the two it ran, so the choice is never silent.
comparing.p4: Hex comparisons ignore case, because hex digits carry no case. Base64 comparisons do not, because base64 does. Passwords are never trimmed — a leading space is part of a password, and stripping it would turn a mismatch into a match.

useCases.title: What people use this for
useCases.p1: Checking a download. A project publishes a SHA-256 sum next to its release; you hash the file's contents and compare. Compare mode does the whole thing in one step: paste the published sum on the right and your computed one on the left.
useCases.p2: Working out why a login fails. You have a bcrypt hash from a database and a password that should match it. Paste both and find out, without writing a script or standing up a server.
useCases.p3: Sizing a cost factor. Raise bcrypt's cost or Argon2's memory and watch how long a single hash takes. Your servers are faster than a browser tab, but the shape of the curve is the same, and it makes the trade-off concrete.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is anything I type sent to a server?
faq.a1: No. Every algorithm here runs as WebAssembly inside your browser, and the page makes no network request while hashing. There is also deliberately no URL parameter carrying the text you hash: a value in a URL ends up in browser history, proxy and server logs, and the referrer header of every outbound link. That said, treat any web tool as untrusted with real credentials — use test passwords.
faq.q2: Can I get the original text back from a hash?
faq.a2: No, and not because this tool refuses to. Hashing discards information; a 128-bit MD5 of a one-megabyte file cannot contain the file. What sites advertising "MD5 decryption" actually do is look your hash up in a table of previously computed ones, which finds common passwords and nothing else. That is exactly the attack salting defeats.
faq.q3: Why does bcrypt give me a different hash every time?
faq.a3: Because it salts. Each run mixes in fresh random bytes, which are stored inside the resulting string, so the same password produces a different hash each time and two users with the same password do not have matching database rows. Use Compare mode rather than eyeballing two hashes — the verifier reads the salt back out and does the right thing.
faq.q4: Which should I use, bcrypt or Argon2?
faq.a4: Argon2id for anything new. It is the current first recommendation, its memory cost defends against hardware bcrypt cannot, and it has no length limit. Choose bcrypt when you need a format with a mature library in every language, or when you are matching a system that already uses it. Both are enormously better than any fast digest.
faq.q5: What does the 72-byte bcrypt limit mean for me?
faq.a5: bcrypt hashes the first 72 bytes of a password and ignores the rest, so two long passphrases sharing a 72-byte prefix produce the same hash. This tool refuses input past that limit rather than truncating it silently. Note that it counts bytes, not characters — an emoji is four bytes, so 18 of them reach the ceiling. Argon2id has no such limit.
faq.a6: For non-adversarial integrity, yes. Checking that a file arrived intact over a flaky connection, or keying a cache, is fine — nobody is crafting a collision to corrupt your cache. It is not safe for anything an attacker touches: colliding MD5 inputs can be produced in seconds on a laptop, which is why it was removed from certificates.
faq.q7: Why is the cost factor capped at 14 when bcrypt allows 31?
faq.a7: The cap is about this page, not about bcrypt. Hashing runs on the same thread that draws the interface, and each cost step doubles the time — 14 already freezes the tab for about a second. Your server has no such constraint and should generally run 10 to 12.

errors.unterminated_string: The string opened at line {line, number}, column {column, number} is never closed.
errors.invalid_escape: {found} at line {line, number}, column {column, number} is not an escape JSON recognises. The valid ones are \" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t and \uXXXX.
errors.invalid_number: The number at line {line, number}, column {column, number} is not written the way JSON requires. A leading zero, a leading +, and a missing digit either side of the point are all rejected.
errors.invalid_literal: {found} at line {line, number}, column {column, number} is not a JSON value. Only true, false and null are spelled out.
errors.control_character: A raw control character sits inside the string at line {line, number}, column {column, number}. Tabs and line breaks have to be written as \t and \n.
errors.trailing_content: The document is already complete at line {line, number}, column {column, number}, but more text follows it.
errors.trailing_comma: The comma at line {line, number}, column {column, number} is followed by the closing bracket. JSON has no trailing commas.
errors.missing_comma: Two values run together at line {line, number}, column {column, number} with no comma between them.
errors.comment: JSON has no comments. One starts at line {line, number}, column {column, number}.
errors.non_standard_quote: The string at line {line, number}, column {column, number} is not wrapped in double quotes. JSON has no single quotes and no curly quotes.
errors.unquoted_key: The key {found} at line {line, number}, column {column, number} is not quoted. Every JSON name is a double-quoted string.
errors.non_standard_literal: {found} at line {line, number}, column {column, number} is not a JSON value. JSON has no NaN, no Infinity and no undefined.
errors.root_not_container: RFC 4627 defines a JSON text as an object or an array, so a bare value at the top level is not a document under it. Switch to RFC 8259 to accept it.
errors.unpaired_surrogate: The string at line {line, number}, column {column, number} holds half of a surrogate pair. That is not valid Unicode and cannot be written as UTF-8, so RFC 8259 refuses it — the other grammars only warn.
errors.repairHint: Turn on Repair and this is corrected for you.
errors.fileUnreadable: That file could not be read.

understanding.title: Understanding JSON formatting
understanding.p1: JSON carries no formatting of its own. Whitespace between tokens has no meaning at all, so the same document can arrive as one unbroken line or spread across a thousand indented ones, and every parser reads them identically. Formatting is entirely for the person looking at it.
understanding.p2: That is why a formatter is really two tools sharing a parser. Beautifying inserts line breaks and indentation so structure becomes visible at a glance; minifying strips every optional byte so the document costs as little as possible to send. Neither changes what the document says.
understanding.p3: Validating is the third thing the same parser gives you for free. A document either matches the grammar or it does not, and when it does not, the useful answer is not “invalid” — it is the line and column where the grammar stopped matching, and what was expected there instead.

whyFormat.title: Why beautify, and why minify
whyFormat.p1: Most JSON that reaches a person came from a machine, and machines emit the compact form. An API response, a log line, a config value pulled out of an environment variable: all of them arrive as a single line that is impossible to read past the first nesting level. Beautifying is how you find the one field you came for.
whyFormat.p2: Minifying runs the other way, and the wins are real but bounded. Indentation is often a fifth to a third of a pretty-printed document, so stripping it is worth doing on anything that crosses a network many times a day. It is not worth doing on anything a person will read, and it is pointless on a response that is already gzipped, where the compressor removes most of that redundancy anyway.
whyFormat.p3: The honest rule is that formatting follows the audience. Files a human edits — configuration, fixtures, seed data — stay beautified and diff cleanly line by line. Payloads only a program reads get minified. Nothing about correctness changes either way, which is exactly why this is a preference rather than a decision to agonise over.

templates.title: Indentation templates
templates.intro: The template decides one thing: what one level of nesting costs. Everything else about the output is the same.
templates.tableCaption: The indentation templates this formatter produces and what each suits
templates.space2BestFor: The default nearly everywhere: JavaScript tooling, npm manifests, most API examples
templates.space3BestFor: Matching a house style that already uses it; rare outside legacy codebases
templates.space4BestFor: Deeply nested documents where two spaces stop being distinguishable, and Python-adjacent projects
templates.tabBestFor: Letting each reader choose their own width, and any repository whose editor config uses tabs
templates.minifiedBestFor: Payloads on the wire, embedded strings, and anything a person will not read
templates.note: Minifying is a separate action rather than a fifth template, because it is not an indentation choice — it removes the line breaks too. Switch the action at the top of the tool and the indentation control goes quiet, since there is nothing left for it to act on.

specs.title: Four specifications, and what actually differs
specs.intro: JSON has been standardised four times, which sounds worse than it is. Three of the four describe the same language; only one of them is genuinely stricter, and it is the oldest.
specs.tableCaption: How each published JSON specification treats a document
specs.rfc8259Here: The default. Additionally refuses a string carrying half of a surrogate pair, because that cannot be encoded as UTF-8.
specs.rfc7159Here: Lifted RFC 4627's restriction on the top level. A lone surrogate is reported as a warning rather than an error.
specs.rfc4627Here: The original definition. A bare string, number, boolean or null at the top level is rejected as not being a JSON text.
specs.ecma404Here: Published alongside RFC 7159 to describe the same grammar, so this tool treats the two identically.
specs.note: If you are unsure, leave it on RFC 8259 — it is what every current parser implements and what “JSON” means in 2026. Reach for RFC 4627 only when you are targeting something genuinely old, such as a strict validator written against the 2006 definition, and want to know in advance that a bare value will be refused.

options.title: Every option, and when to use it
options.intro: The defaults — beautify at two spaces, RFC 8259, repair off, document order, output as-is — are what you want most of the time. The rest exist for the cases where the document is broken, the receiving system is stricter, or the output has to survive a narrower channel.
options.tableCaption: What each control does and when it is worth changing
options.indentDoes: Sets what one nesting level costs: two, three or four spaces, or a tab.
options.indentWhen: The output goes into a repository whose style differs from the two-space default.
options.specDoes: Chooses which published grammar the document is held to.
options.specWhen: You are targeting a parser written against an older definition, or want a lone surrogate treated as fatal.
options.repairDoes: Accepts the usual non-standard extras — trailing commas, comments, bare keys, single and curly quotes, NaN and Infinity, hex and malformed numbers — and writes valid JSON out.
options.repairWhen: You pasted something that came from a config file, a Python REPL, or a document someone edited by hand.
options.sortKeysDoes: Reorders every object's members by name, all the way down.
options.sortKeysWhen: You are about to diff two documents, or want a stable order for a checksum or a fixture.
options.escapeUnicodeDoes: Rewrites every character above ASCII as a \uXXXX escape.
options.escapeUnicodeWhen: The output travels through something that mangles UTF-8 — an old logging pipeline, a terminal paste, a header value.
options.interactionNote: The controls constrain each other, and the interface follows suit rather than lying about it. Minifying removes every space, so the indentation control greys out. Validating reports on the document instead of rewriting it, so indentation, key sorting and Unicode escaping all go quiet — none of them would have anything to act on.
options.defaultsNote: Repair deserves one caveat. It only touches things whose intent is unambiguous: a comma before a closing bracket can only be a trailing comma, and a bare word where a key belongs can only be an unquoted key. It will not guess at an unterminated string, because the closing quote could belong anywhere, and it will not invent a missing bracket. When it does change something, the report says exactly what it changed and how many times.

reading.title: Reading an error
reading.p1: Every failure comes back with a line and a column, counted the way you would count them: from one, in characters. That last part matters more than it sounds. An emoji earlier in the line is one character to you but two units to the engine underneath, and a formatter that counts the engine's way reports every later column one place too far along.
reading.p2: The message names what the grammar wanted and what it found instead, because “unexpected token” on its own sends you reading the whole document. Knowing that a colon was expected at line 12, column 9, and a comma turned up, usually points straight at the missing quote two lines above.
reading.p3: When the problem is one Repair understands, the message says so rather than leaving you to guess. Trailing commas, comments, bare keys, non-standard quotes and NaN all carry that hint; unterminated strings and missing brackets do not, because no automatic fix for them would be safe.

howItWorks.title: How our formatter works
howItWorks.p1: Everything on this page runs on your device. The document is read by a parser written for this tool rather than handed to the browser's own JSON.parse, and there is no server call and nothing stored.
howItWorks.p2: That choice buys three things. JSON.parse reports failures through an error message that every engine words differently — some carry a line and column, some do not — so a formatter built on it gives a different answer in Chrome than in Safari. It also has no lenient mode, which is what Repair needs. And it routes every number through a double, which silently rounds any integer past 9,007,199,254,740,992; keeping the literal exactly as written is the only way a formatter can promise it did not quietly change your data.
howItWorks.p3: The rest follows from that. Strings are decoded once and re-escaped canonically on the way out, so the output is byte-identical whichever escapes the input happened to use. A byte order mark at the start is ignored, as the specification permits. Nesting is capped at 512 levels and input at one megabyte, both reported as ordinary messages rather than a frozen tab.

useCases.title: Use cases
useCases.p1: Reading an API response is the common one. Paste the single line your terminal printed, beautify it, and the shape you were looking for is visible immediately — including which fields are null and which are missing altogether.
useCases.p2: Fixing a config file someone hand-edited is the second. A trailing comma in a tsconfig, a comment in a package manifest, smart quotes pasted out of a chat message: turn on Repair, and the output is the same document with the damage undone and a list of what changed.
useCases.p3: Beyond that: sorting keys before diffing two fixtures so the diff shows real changes rather than reordering, minifying a payload before embedding it in a source file, escaping non-ASCII so a document survives a pipeline that mangles UTF-8, and checking whether a large integer id is one your consumers will round.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does formatting change what my JSON means?
faq.a1: No. Whitespace between tokens carries no meaning in JSON, so beautifying and minifying produce documents that every parser reads identically. Sorting keys is the one option that rewrites something a program could notice — object member order is not significant in JSON, but a few systems do observe it, so it is off by default.
faq.a2: No. Files are read with the browser's File API and everything is parsed and written on your device. The page makes no network request while formatting, and nothing you paste, open, or download is transmitted.
faq.q3: Why does my big number survive here but not in my code?
faq.a3: Because this tool keeps number literals exactly as written instead of routing them through a double. JSON.parse cannot: any integer past 9,007,199,254,740,992 loses precision the moment it is read, which is why a 19-digit id often comes back off by one. The report flags any literal that would round, so you can see it before your consumers do.
faq.a4: Trailing commas, missing commas between values, // and /* */ comments, unquoted keys, single and curly quotes, NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, undefined, Python's True, False and None, hex numbers, leading zeros, leading plus signs, a missing digit either side of a decimal point, unknown backslash escapes, and raw control characters inside strings. It stops short of anything ambiguous: it will not close a string for you or invent a missing bracket.
faq.a5: RFC 8259 unless you know otherwise — it is what every current parser implements. RFC 7159 and ECMA-404 describe the same grammar and behave identically here. RFC 4627 is the 2006 original and is the only genuinely stricter option: it requires an object or an array at the top level, so a bare string or number is refused.
faq.q6: Why is a duplicate key a warning rather than an error?
faq.a6: Because the grammar allows it. Every specification says member names SHOULD be unique but none requires it, so a document with a repeated name is valid JSON. What is unpredictable is what a parser does with it — most keep the last occurrence, some keep the first, a few error — which is exactly why it is worth telling you about.
faq.q7: Can I share a formatted document as a link?
faq.a7: Yes, for short ones. The action, indentation, specification and each toggle all travel in the URL, along with up to 2,048 characters of text, so a link opens on the same settings and the same document. Anything longer is better handed over as a file — and it never leaves your machine either way.
